newsitem.title: USA: U.S. food aid to North Korea a first step - experts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. food aid to North Korea a first step - experts.

text.p: The thousands of tons of U.S. food aid to North Korea just approved by the Clinton administration will help the famine-stricken nation for only a short while, and much more aid will be necessary to get the country on its feet again, relief experts said on Thursday.

"This is really just the first step towards meeting what the real need is," said Ken Casey, senior vice president of the international relief group World Vision. "This should not be the full extent of the U.S. committment to North Korea."

The State Department announced on Wednesday that in response to an appeal from the U.N. World Food Programme for $41.5 million to provide 100,000 metric tons of food to North Korea, the United States will send an extra $10 million worth of food aid to the strapped communist nation.
Washington provided $8.5 million in total aid to North Korea last year, including $6.2 million worth of food.

The U.N. World Food Programme has estimated that North Korea's food shortfall could be as high as 2.3 million metric tons. Two consecutive years of devastating floods that struck already deteriorating farms have caused widespread, life-threatening food shortage problems.

The latest U.S. aid will provide about 33,000 tons of food -- 5,000 tons of high protein corn soy blend for young children and 6,600 tons of rice and 20,780 tons of corn to farm families in the flood-drenched areas. Experts said the food will probably last about two months.
Relief groups, who have been pressuring the administration for some time to approve more aid, praised the latest decision but said the government has to follow up with more help.
While making no commitment to approve more aid, a State Department official said that any future appeals for more humanitarian assistance to North Korea would be considered.

"There is a serious food problem in North Korea ... We are willing to consider requests for assistance on a humanitarian basis and have responded on a humantarian basis to several appeals now," said the official.

The Agency for International Development will be in charge of the latest tranche of aid, and AID officials said they are beginning the process immediately in order for the food to reach the hungry country as soon as possible.

"We will move out pretty quickly, and we would expect that about 90 days from now, our food will be there for distribution," said Len Rogers, acting assistant administrator for AID's Bureau for Humanitarian Response.
The U.S. food aid is targeted to reach close to two million people in North Korea, including a third of the country's young children under five.
